# Community similarity {#sec-community-similarity}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 10, dpi = 300)
```

Beta diversity quantifies the dissimilarity between communities (multiple
samples), as opposed to alpha diversity, which focuses on variation within a
community (one sample). In microbiome research, commonly used metrics
of beta diversity include:

- Bray-Curtis index (for compositional data) [@Bray1957]
- Jaccard index (for presence/absence data, ignoring abundance information)
[@Jaccard1912]
- Aitchison distance (Euclidean distance for clr-transformed abundances, aiming
to avoid the compositionality bias) [@Aitchison1986]
- UniFrac distance (takes into account the phylogenetic tree information)
[@Lozupone2005].

Notably, only some of these measures are actual _distances_, as this is a
mathematical concept whose definition is not satisfied by certain ecological
measures, such as the Bray-Curtis index. Therefore, the terms dissimilarity and
beta diversity are preferred.

The table below lists commonly used combinations of assay type and beta
diversity metric.

| Method description          | Assay type          | Beta diversity metric |
|:---------------------------:|:-------------------:|:---------------------:|
| Quantitative profiling      | Absolute counts     | Bray-Curtis           |
| Relative profiling          | Relative abundances | Bray-Curtis           |
| Aitchison distance          | Absolute counts     | Aitchison             |
| Aitchison distance          | clr                 | Euclidean             |
| Robust Aitchison distance   | rclr                | Euclidean             |
| Presence/Absence similarity | Relative abundances | Jaccard               |
| Presence/Absence similarity | Absolute counts     | Jaccard               |
| Phylogenetic distance       | Rarefied counts     | UniFrac               |

::: {.callout-tip }
## Dissimilarity or distance?

The terms dissimilarity and distance are often used interchangeably, but they
have distinct meanings.

All distance metrics are also dissimilarity metrics, but not all dissimilarity
metrics are distance metrics.

Dissimilarity is a broader concept that measures how different two samples
are. Dissimilarity metrics do not necessarily fulfill the requirements of
distances. For instance, Bray-Curtis is a dissimilarity metric: it is
symmetric, but it does not satisfy the triangle inequality.

Distance metrics, for example Euclidean distance, measure how far apart two
samples are. A distance is always symmetric, meaning that the distance from A
to B equals the distance from B to A. Moreover, it satisfies the triangle
inequality: the direct distance between two points is never longer than a
detour through a third point.
:::

In practice, beta diversity is usually represented as a `dist` object. Such an
object is a triangular matrix where the distance between each pair of samples
is encoded by a specific cell (@fig-beta-workflow). This distance matrix can
then undergo ordination, which is an important ecological tool to reduce the
dimensionality of data for a more efficient analysis and visualization.
Ordination techniques aim to capture as much essential information from the
data as possible and turn it into a lower dimensional representation. While dimension reduction
inevitably results in some information loss, commonly utilized ordination
techniques aim to optimally preserve meaningful patterns of sample similarity,
with the definition of “optimal” varying by method.

```{r}
#| label: fig-beta-workflow
#| fig-cap: "From abundances to an ordination. Beta diversity compares the abundance profiles of each pair of samples (1) and stores the dissimilarities, here Bray-Curtis, in a triangular matrix (2). Ordination, here PCoA, places the samples in a low-dimensional space so that similar samples lie close to each other (3). Toy data."
#| fig-alt: "Three panels from left to right. Panel 1 is a tile grid of six samples by five taxa shaded by abundance; panel 2 is a triangular matrix of pairwise dissimilarities with values printed in the cells; panel 3 is a scatter plot of the six samples on PCoA 1 and PCoA 2, colored by Group 1 and Group 2."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
# Toy data; run in local() so that helper objects do not leak into later
# chunks.
local({
    # Toy abundance table: 6 samples (two groups) x 5 taxa
    counts <- matrix(
        c(
            30, 25, 5, 10, 30,
            40, 10, 10, 5, 35,
            20, 35, 12, 20, 13,
            8, 15, 35, 30, 12,
            15, 5, 30, 20, 30,
            5, 20, 25, 45, 5
        ),
        nrow = 6, byrow = TRUE,
        dimnames = list(paste0("S", 1:6), paste0("Taxon ", LETTERS[1:5]))
    )
    group <- rep(c("Group 1", "Group 2"), each = 3)
    d <- vegan::vegdist(counts, method = "bray")
    dm <- as.matrix(d)
    # Abundance table
    tab <- data.frame(
        sample = factor(rep(rownames(counts), ncol(counts)),
            levels = rev(rownames(counts))
        ),
        taxon = rep(colnames(counts), each = nrow(counts)),
        value = as.vector(counts)
    )
    p1 <- ggplot(tab, aes(taxon, sample, fill = value)) +
        geom_tile(colour = "white") +
        scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f2f2f2", high = "#0087af", guide = "none") +
        labs(title = "1. Abundance table", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(
            axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
            panel.grid = element_blank()
        )
    # Lower triangle of the dissimilarity matrix
    dd <- data.frame(
        s1 = factor(rep(rownames(dm), ncol(dm)), levels = rownames(dm)),
        s2 = factor(rep(colnames(dm), each = nrow(dm)),
            levels = rev(colnames(dm))
        ),
        value = as.vector(dm)
    )
    dd <- dd[as.integer(dd$s1) < (nrow(dm) + 1 - as.integer(dd$s2)), ]
    p2 <- ggplot(dd, aes(s1, s2, fill = value)) +
        geom_tile(colour = "white") +
        geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", value)), size = 3) +
        scale_fill_gradient(low = "#fff3e0", high = "#E69F00", guide = "none") +
        labs(title = "2. Dissimilarities", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
    # PCoA
    pcoa <- cmdscale(d, k = 2, eig = TRUE)
    expl <- round(100 * pcoa$eig[1:2] / sum(pcoa$eig[pcoa$eig > 0]))
    ord <- data.frame(pcoa$points, sample = rownames(counts), group = group)
    p3 <- ggplot(ord, aes(X1, X2, colour = group)) +
        geom_point(size = 3) +
        geom_text(aes(label = sample),
            vjust = -1, size = 3.2,
            show.legend = FALSE
        ) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00"), name = NULL) +
        scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.25)) +
        labs(
            title = "3. Ordination (PCoA)",
            x = paste0("PCoA 1 (", expl[1], "%)"),
            y = paste0("PCoA 2 (", expl[2], "%)")
        ) +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text = element_blank())
    p1 + p2 + p3 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1, 1))
})
```

Based on the type of algorithm, ordination methods in microbiome research can
be generally divided into two categories:

- unsupervised ordination
- supervised ordination

The former includes Principal Coordinate Analysis (PCoA) [@Gower1966] and
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) [@Pearson1901; @Hotelling1933], whereas the
latter
is mainly represented by distance-based redundancy analysis (dbRDA)
[@Legendre1999]. First, we will discuss unsupervised ordination
methods and then proceed to supervised ones.

Let us now prepare some demonstration data for the practical examples.

```{r}
#| label: prep_tse

# Load mia and import sample dataset
library(mia)
data("GlobalPatterns", package = "mia")
tse <- GlobalPatterns

# Beta diversity metrics like Bray-Curtis are often
# applied to relabundances
tse <- transformAssay(
    tse,
    assay.type = "counts", method = "relabundance"
)

# Other metrics like Aitchison to clr-transformed data
tse <- transformAssay(
    tse,
    assay.type = "counts", method = "clr", pseudocount = 0.5
)

# Add group information Feces yes/no
tse$Group <- ifelse(tse$SampleType == "Feces", "Fecal", "Non-fecal")
```

::: {.callout-caution }
## Common mistake in Jaccard index

The standard Jaccard index is calculated based on a presence/absence table.
However, a common mistake is using the quantitative version instead. By
default, the function `vegdist()` from the `r BiocStyle::CRANpkg("vegan")`
package [@R_vegan] computes the abundance-weighted Jaccard
dissimilarity, which is similar to Bray-Curtis. This can be controlled using
the `binary` parameter.

When calculating the Jaccard index with `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("mia")`'s
functions (including `getPERMANOVA()` and `addRDA()`), it defaults to standard
presence/absence version:

```
tse <- addDissimilarity(tse, assay.type = "counts", method = "jaccard")
```
... or if you want to be more explicit, you can transform the data to
presence/absence scale and then calculate the Jaccard index:

```
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "pa")
tse <- addDissimilarity(tse, assay.type = "pa", method = "jaccard")
```

:::

## Dissimilarity

Perhaps the simplest way to analyze dissimilarity is to calculate a
dissimilarity matrix. In this matrix, each sample is compared with every
other sample based on the specified dissimilarity method. The result includes
a single number for each sample-pair. This number is an indication of how similar or
dissimilar the microbial communities are.

One can calculate a dissimilarity matrix with `*Dissimilarity()` functions.
Here we use `addDissimilarity()` that adds the matrix to the `metadata` slot.
We calculate UniFrac dissimilarity that takes into account phylogenetic
distances.

```{r}
#| label: diss_matrix

tse <- addDissimilarity(tse, assay.type = "counts", method = "unifrac")
```

The dissimilarities can then be visualized with a heatmap
(@fig-community-dissimilarity-heatmap). Here we also add sample information to
the plot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-dissimilarity-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Heatmap of pairwise UniFrac dissimilarities between the GlobalPatterns samples. Samples are ordered by seriation and split by sample type."
#| fig-alt: "Square heatmap with the samples on both axes, where cell color shows the UniFrac dissimilarity of each sample pair. Samples are split into blocks by sample type, and samples of the same type tend to be the most similar to each other."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 12

library(miaViz)

# Wrap long sample type names
tse_plot <- tse
tse_plot[["SampleType"]] <- factor(
    tse_plot[["SampleType"]],
    labels = gsub(" \\(", "\n(", levels(tse_plot[["SampleType"]]))
)

plotDissimilarity(tse_plot, name = "unifrac", col.var = "SampleType")
```

From the heatmap, we can observe that samples within the same sample type are
the most similar to each other. `plotDissimilarity()` orders the samples by
seriation of the dissimilarities (by default, their angular order in a
multidimensional scaling; see the `sort.method` argument) and splits them by
sample type.

## Divergence {#sec-divergence}

The divergence measure refers to a difference in community composition
between the given sample(s) and a reference sample. This can be evaluated with
`addDivergence()`. The reference and the dissimilarity measure can be
specified with the `reference` and `method` arguments, respectively. The
result is stored in the `divergence` column of `colData`.

```{r}
#| label: add_divergence

tse <- addDivergence(
    tse,
    assay.type = "counts",
    reference = "median"
)
tse$divergence |> head()
```

## Group comparison (PERMANOVA) {#sec-permanova}

PERMANOVA (Permutational Multivariate Analysis of Variance) [@Anderson2001] can
be seen as a non-parametric, multivariate extension of ANOVA (Analysis of
Variance). It is used to compare groups in multivariate data and to assess
whether a variable explains differences in the data. PERMANOVA first calculates
the dissimilarities between samples, then compares the centroids (multivariate
means) of each group to determine if they differ significantly.

PERMANOVA determines statistical significance by permuting (randomly shuffling)
group labels many times (@fig-permanova-idea). By comparing the observed test
statistic to those from the permutations, it assesses if the observed group
differences are likely due to chance, without relying on parametric
assumptions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-permanova-idea
#| fig-cap: "The idea of PERMANOVA. The test statistic (pseudo-F) compares the distances between group centroids (crosses) to the spread of samples around their own centroid (left). Permuting the group labels gives the distribution of pseudo-F when groups do not differ; the p-value is the proportion of permutations with a pseudo-F at least as large as the observed one (right). Toy data."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. Left: a scatter plot of two colored groups of toy samples on two PCoA axes, with a black cross at each group centroid and faint lines from every sample to its centroid. Right: a gray histogram of pseudo-F values from permutations, with a vertical line marking the observed pseudo-F and a label giving its value and the p-value."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
# Toy data; run in local() so that helper objects do not leak into later
# chunks.
local({
    set.seed(1)
    # Toy data: 10 samples per group, 8 taxa; group means differ
    n <- 10
    mu1 <- c(30, 25, 15, 10, 8, 5, 4, 3)
    mu2 <- c(12, 15, 25, 20, 10, 8, 6, 4)
    counts <- rbind(
        t(replicate(n, rpois(8, mu1 * exp(rnorm(8, 0, 0.5))))),
        t(replicate(n, rpois(8, mu2 * exp(rnorm(8, 0, 0.5)))))
    )
    group <- factor(rep(c("Group 1", "Group 2"), each = n))
    d <- vegan::vegdist(counts, method = "bray")
    # Pseudo-F statistic of PERMANOVA (Anderson 2001)
    pseudo_f <- function(d, g) {
        d2 <- as.matrix(d)^2
        N <- length(g)
        a <- nlevels(g)
        ss_tot <- sum(d2[upper.tri(d2)]) / N
        ss_w <- sum(vapply(levels(g), function(l) {
            i <- which(g == l)
            sum(d2[i, i][upper.tri(d2[i, i])]) / length(i)
        }, numeric(1)))
        ((ss_tot - ss_w) / (a - 1)) / (ss_w / (N - a))
    }
    f_obs <- pseudo_f(d, group)
    f_null <- replicate(999, pseudo_f(d, sample(group)))
    p_val <- (sum(f_null >= f_obs) + 1) / (length(f_null) + 1)
    # Ordination with group centroids and "spokes" to each sample
    pcoa <- cmdscale(d, k = 2)
    ord <- data.frame(PC1 = pcoa[, 1], PC2 = pcoa[, 2], group = group)
    cen <- aggregate(cbind(PC1, PC2) ~ group, data = ord, FUN = mean)
    ord <- merge(ord, cen, by = "group", suffixes = c("", ".c"))
    cols <- c("Group 1" = "#0072B2", "Group 2" = "#D55E00")
    p1 <- ggplot(ord, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = group)) +
        geom_segment(aes(xend = PC1.c, yend = PC2.c), alpha = 0.4) +
        geom_point(size = 2.5) +
        geom_point(
            data = cen, shape = 4, size = 5, stroke = 2,
            colour = "black"
        ) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = cols, name = NULL) +
        labs(
            title = "Within-group spread vs. distance between centroids",
            x = "PCoA 1", y = "PCoA 2"
        ) +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(
            legend.position = "bottom", axis.text = element_blank(),
            plot.title = element_text(size = 12)
        )
    p2 <- ggplot(data.frame(f = f_null), aes(f)) +
        geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
        geom_vline(xintercept = f_obs, colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1) +
        annotate("text",
            x = f_obs, y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 1.05,
            label = sprintf("Observed F = %.1f\np = %.3f", f_obs, p_val),
            colour = "#D55E00", size = 3.8
        ) +
        labs(
            title = "Pseudo-F after permuting the group labels",
            x = "Pseudo-F", y = "Permutations"
        ) +
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12))
    p1 + p2
})
```

Since PERMANOVA relies on comparing centroids, it assumes that the groups have
similar within-group variation, i.e., homogeneous multivariate dispersions
[@Anderson2006]. If
this assumption isn’t met, a significant result may reflect differences in
dispersion rather than in centroids, so it’s important to check this
assumption before drawing conclusions.

```{r}
#| label: permanova

set.seed(123)
res <- getPERMANOVA(
    tse,
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    formula = x ~ SampleType
)
res
```

The output includes both PERMANOVA and homogeneity results. When PERMANOVA
results are significant, we check the homogeneity results to ensure
reliability. The homogeneity test measures group dispersions which are the
average distances between samples and their group centroids. A non-significant
homogeneity result indicates that groups have similar within-group variability,
i.e., the group dispersions are homogeneous, which is desired in PERMANOVA.

In our case, PERMANOVA results are significant; however, the homogeneity test
shows a significant difference in group dispersion. This
suggests that the observed differences may be influenced by unequal variability
among groups, and therefore, caution is needed when interpreting the PERMANOVA
result. The effect of _SampleType_ on microbial composition may be confounded
by dispersion differences.

PERMANOVA and distance-based redundancy analysis (dbRDA) are closely related,
and they often give similar results. However, their assumptions are different;
while PERMANOVA is a non-parametric method, dbRDA assumes linear relationships
in the dissimilarity matrix. In addition, dbRDA can be used more broadly as the
ordination can also be visualized.

## Unsupervised ordination {#sec-unsupervised-ordination}

Unsupervised ordination methods analyze variation in the data without
additional information on covariates or other supervision of the model. Among
the different approaches, Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) and non-metric MDS
(NMDS) [@Kruskal1964] can be regarded as the standard. Metric MDS is also
known as Principal Coordinate Analysis (PCoA).
For this demonstration, we will analyze beta diversity in `GlobalPatterns`
[@Caporaso2011] ([@sec-data-globalpatterns]), and observe the variation
between stool samples and samples of differing origin.

### Comparing communities {#sec-comparing-communities-by-beta-diversity-analysis}

A typical comparison of community compositions starts with calculating the
dissimilarities between the samples, for example with the Bray-Curtis index
on the relative abundances. The samples are then ordinated with MDS, and the
groups are compared visually in a 2D ordination plot. The `addMDS()` and
`addNMDS()` functions calculate the dissimilarities and the ordination in one
step.

The choice of the dissimilarity metric is important. It is selected with the
`method` argument of `addMDS()` and `addNMDS()`. All standard metrics are
available; see `?getDissimilarity` for the full list. The results are stored
in the `reducedDim` slot of the TreeSE.

```{r}
#| label: addMDS

# Load package to plot ordinations
library(miaViz)

# Run PCoA on relabundance assay with Bray-Curtis distances
tse <- addMDS(
    tse,
    method = "bray",
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    name = "MDS_bray"
)
```

Sample dissimilarity can be visualized on a lower-dimensional display
(typically 2D) using the `plotOrdination()` function from the
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("miaViz")` package.
This also provides tools to incorporate additional information encoded by
color, shape, size and other aesthetics. Can you find any difference between
the groups in @fig-community-mds-bray?

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-mds-bray
#| fig-cap: "MDS (PCoA) plot based on the Bray-Curtis dissimilarities of relative abundances in the GlobalPatterns dataset. Points are colored by group (fecal or non-fecal sample), and axis labels show the proportion of variance explained."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of the samples on the first two MDS axes, with the percentage of variance explained in the axis labels. Points are colored by whether the sample is fecal or not."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

# Create ggplot object with explained variance in the axis labels
p <- plotOrdination(
    tse, "MDS_bray",
    colour.by = "Group",
    add.expl.var = TRUE
)

p
```

To further visualize the differences between the groups, we can add boxplots
that display the distribution of the scores with respect to each group
(@fig-community-mds-bray-boxplots).

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-mds-bray-boxplots
#| fig-cap: "Bray-Curtis MDS plot of the GlobalPatterns dataset with marginal boxplots showing the distribution of the scores on each axis for fecal and non-fecal samples."
#| fig-alt: "The same MDS scatter plot colored by fecal versus non-fecal samples, with boxplots along the top and right margins comparing the two groups' scores on the horizontal and vertical axes."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7

library(ggExtra)

# Legend below, so that it is not between the plot and the boxplots
p <- p + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p <- ggMarginal(p, type = "boxplot", groupFill = TRUE)
p
```


A few combinations of beta diversity metrics and assay types are typically
used. For instance, Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and Euclidean distance are often
applied to the relative abundance and the clr assays, respectively. Besides
**beta diversity metric** and **assay type**, the **PCoA algorithm** is also a
variable that should be considered. Below, we show how the choice of these
three factors can affect the resulting lower-dimensional data.

```{r}
#| label: mds-nmds_comparison1
#| results: hide

# Run NMDS on relabundance assay with Bray-Curtis distances
tse <- addNMDS(
    tse,
    method = "bray",
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    name = "NMDS_bray"
)

# Run MDS on clr assay with Aitchison distances
tse <- addMDS(
    tse,
    method = "euclidean",
    assay.type = "clr",
    name = "MDS_aitchison"
)

# Run NMDS on clr assay with Euclidean distances
tse <- addNMDS(
    tse,
    method = "euclidean",
    assay.type = "clr",
    name = "NMDS_aitchison"
)
```

Multiple ordination plots are combined into a multi-panel plot
(@fig-community-mds-nmds-comparison) with the
`r BiocStyle::CRANpkg("patchwork")` package, so that
different methods can be compared to find similarities between them or select
the most suitable one to visualize beta diversity in the light of the research
question.

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-mds-nmds-comparison
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of MDS and NMDS plots based on the Bray-Curtis or Aitchison distances on the GlobalPatterns dataset: (A) MDS, Bray-Curtis; (B) MDS, Aitchison; (C) NMDS, Bray-Curtis; (D) NMDS, Aitchison. Points are colored by group (fecal or non-fecal sample)."
#| fig-alt: "Grid of four scatter plots: MDS and NMDS ordinations with Bray-Curtis and with Aitchison distances. In every panel, points are colored by fecal or non-fecal sample, with a shared legend."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7

# Load package for multi-panel plotting
library(patchwork)

# Generate plots for all 4 reducedDims
p1 <- plotOrdination(
    tse, "MDS_bray",
    colour.by = "Group", add.expl.var = TRUE
) +
    labs(title = "MDS, Bray-Curtis")
p2 <- plotOrdination(
    tse, "MDS_aitchison",
    colour.by = "Group", add.expl.var = TRUE
) +
    labs(title = "MDS, Aitchison")
p3 <- plotOrdination(tse, "NMDS_bray", colour.by = "Group") +
    labs(title = "NMDS, Bray-Curtis")
p4 <- plotOrdination(tse, "NMDS_aitchison", colour.by = "Group") +
    labs(title = "NMDS, Aitchison")

# Generate multi-panel plot
wrap_plots(p1, p2, p3, p4) +
    plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
    plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

The _UniFrac_ method is a special case, as it requires the phylogenetic tree
of the features. `addMDS()` uses the tree in `rowTree(tse)` by default
(@fig-community-mds-unifrac).

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-mds-unifrac
#| fig-cap: "UniFrac distances scaled by MDS of the GlobalPatterns dataset. Points are colored by group (fecal or non-fecal sample)."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of the samples on the first two MDS axes based on UniFrac distances, with points colored by fecal or non-fecal sample."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

tse <- addMDS(
    tse,
    method = "unifrac",
    name = "MDS_unifrac",
    assay.type = "counts"
)

plotOrdination(tse, "MDS_unifrac", colour.by = "Group", add.expl.var = TRUE)
```

### Rarefaction {#sec-rarefaction_ordination}

Background on rarefaction [@Sanders1968; @Hurlbert1971] is provided in
[@sec-rarefaction]. For rarefaction in beta diversity analysis, see
@Schloss2024rarefaction1.

Let us first convert the count assay to centered log ratio (clr) assay and
calculate MDS with Aitchison distance without rarefaction:

```{r}
#| label: Aitchison_distance_without_rarefaction

# Centered log-ratio transformation to properly apply Aitchison distance
tse <- transformAssay(
    tse,
    assay.type = "counts",
    method = "clr",
    pseudocount = 1,
    name = "clr_pc1"
)

# Run MDS on clr assay with Aitchison distance
tse <- addMDS(
    tse,
    method = "euclidean",
    assay.type = "clr_pc1",
    name = "MDS_aitchison_pc1"
)
```

Then let's do the same with rarefaction:

```{r}
#| label: rarefied_mds

# Define custom transformation function
clr <- function(x) {
    vegan::decostand(x, method = "clr", pseudocount = 1)
}

# Run transformation after rarefactions before calculating the beta diversity
tse <- addMDS(
    tse,
    assay.type = "counts",
    method = "euclidean",
    niter = 10, # Number of iterations
    sample = min(colSums(assay(tse, "counts"))), # Rarefaction depth
    transf = clr, # Applied transformation
    name = "MDS_aitchison_rarefied"
)
```

Now we are ready to plot the non-rarefied and rarefied MDS plots side-by-side
(@fig-community-mds-rarefaction).

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-mds-rarefaction
#| fig-cap: "MDS plots based on Aitchison distances of the GlobalPatterns dataset without rarefaction (left) and with rarefaction (right). Points are colored by sample type."
#| fig-alt: "Two scatter plots side by side, showing Aitchison MDS ordinations of the samples without rarefaction (left) and with rarefaction (right). Points are colored by sample type, with a shared legend."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4
#| column: page

# Generate plots for non-rarefied and rarefied Aitchison distances scaled by MDS
p1 <- plotOrdination(tse, "MDS_aitchison_pc1", colour.by = "SampleType") +
    labs(title = "Without rarefaction", colour = "Sample type")
p2 <- plotOrdination(tse, "MDS_aitchison_rarefied", colour.by = "SampleType") +
    labs(title = "With rarefaction", colour = "Sample type")

# Generate multi-panel plot
wrap_plots(p1, p2) +
    plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

The same can be done more compactly with `lapply()`, which creates one plot
for each ordination. This is convenient when comparing more than two
ordinations, as only the vector of names needs to be extended:

```{r}
#| label: mds_rarefaction_lapply
#| eval: false

# One plot for each ordination, combined into a multi-panel plot
plots <- lapply(
    c("MDS_aitchison_pc1", "MDS_aitchison_rarefied"),
    function(name) plotOrdination(tse, name, colour.by = "SampleType")
)
wrap_plots(plots) +
    plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Note

Sometimes features are filtered before ordination. Features that hardly vary
carry little information and mainly add noise. With `addMDS()`, the `ntop`
argument keeps only the given number of features with the highest variance. By
default, all features are used.

:::

When rarefaction is not done, the `getDissimilarity()` utilizes
`vegan::vegdist()` function while in rarefaction `vegan::avgdist()` is applied.
The argument `sample` is set to the smallest metagenomic reads count across
all samples. This ensures that no sample will be removed during the rarefaction
process.

The argument `niter` sets the number of rarefaction rounds. By default
(`niter = NULL`), no rarefaction is applied; here 10 iterations is often
sufficient for beta diversity calculations. To use transformations after the
rarefaction of the samples and before the beta diversity calculation, we can
use the argument `transf`.

The `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("mia")` package's `addAlpha()` and
`getDissimilarity()` functions support rarefaction in alpha and beta diversity
calculations. Additionally, the `rarefyAssay()` function allows random
subsampling of a given assay within a `TreeSummarizedExperiment` dataset.

### Other methods {#sec-other-ord-methods}

Other dimension reduction methods, such as PCA [@Pearson1901; @Hotelling1933]
and robust PCA, are also available. PCA is calculated with `addPCA()` from
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("mia")` and shown in @fig-community-pca.

Nonlinear methods such as t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE)
[@vanderMaaten2008] and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)
[@McInnes2018] are available in the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("scater")` package
[@McCarthy2017] (see the list at the end of this chapter). They are rarely
used for microbiome data, and we do not show examples here: the result
depends strongly on the tuning parameters and the random seed, and the
distances between groups of samples in the plot are not interpretable.

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-pca
#| fig-cap: "PCA plot of the clr-transformed abundances in the GlobalPatterns dataset containing samples from different sources. Points are colored by group (fecal or non-fecal sample), and axis labels show the proportion of variance explained."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of the samples on the first two principal components, with the percentage of variance explained in the axis labels. Points are colored by fecal or non-fecal sample."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

tse <- addPCA(
    tse,
    name = "PCA",
    assay.type = "clr",
    ncomponents = 10
)

# Visualize the result
plotOrdination(tse, "PCA", colour.by = "Group", add.expl.var = TRUE)
```

A scree plot shows how much variance each component explains
(@fig-community-pca-scree). It helps to decide how many components are worth
interpreting: typically those before the curve levels off.

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-pca-scree
#| fig-cap: "Scree plot of the PCA of the clr-transformed GlobalPatterns data. Each point is the eigenvalue (explained variance) of one principal component."
#| fig-alt: "Line plot with the principal components 1 to 10 on the x-axis and their eigenvalues on the y-axis. The eigenvalues drop steeply over the first three components and then level off."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4

plotScree(tse, "PCA")
```

Robust Aitchison PCA (RPCA) [@Martino2019] is a PCA for compositional data
with many zeros. It uses the robust clr (rclr) transformation, which is
calculated from the non-zero values only, and treats the zeros as missing
values that are filled in by matrix completion. Unlike the clr
transformation, it does not need a pseudocount. RPCA is calculated with
`addRPCA()` (@fig-community-rpca). The same method is extended to multiple
omics in Joint-RPCA ([@sec-unsupervised-multiomics]).

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-rpca
#| fig-cap: "Robust Aitchison PCA (RPCA) of the GlobalPatterns dataset. Points are colored by group (fecal or non-fecal sample), and axis labels show the proportion of variance explained."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of the samples on the first two RPCA components, with the percentage of variance explained in the axis labels. Points are colored by fecal or non-fecal sample."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

# rclr without imputation: RPCA itself handles the zeros
tse <- transformAssay(
    tse,
    assay.type = "counts",
    method = "rclr",
    impute = FALSE
)
tse <- addRPCA(tse, assay.type = "rclr", name = "RPCA")

plotOrdination(tse, "RPCA", colour.by = "Group", add.expl.var = TRUE)
```

### Explained variance

The percentage of explained variance is typically shown in PCA ordination
plots. This quantifies the proportion of overall variance in the data that is
captured by the PCA axes, or how well the ordination axes reflect the original
distances.

Sometimes a similar measure is shown for MDS/PCoA. However, the interpretation
is generally different, hence we do not recommend using it. PCA is a special
case of PCoA with Euclidean distances. With non-Euclidean dissimilarities PCoA
uses a trick where the pointwise dissimilarities are first cast into
similarities in a Euclidean space (with some information loss i.e., stress) and
then projected to the maximal variance axes. In this case, the maximal variance
axes do not directly reflect the correspondence of the projected distances and
original distances, as they do for PCA.

In typical use cases, we would like to know how well the ordination
reflects the original similarity structures; then the quantity of interest is
the so-called "stress" function, which measures the difference in pairwise
similarities between the data points in the original (high-dimensional) vs.
projected (low-dimensional) space.

Hence, we propose that for PCoA and other ordination methods, users would
report relative stress, which varies within the unit interval and is better if
smaller. This can be calculated as shown below.

```{r}
#| label: relstress

# Quantify dissimilarities in the original feature space
d0 <- as.matrix(getDissimilarity(t(assay(tse, "relabundance")), "bray"))

# PCoA Ordination
tse <- addMDS(
    tse,
    name = "PCoA",
    method = "bray",
    assay.type = "relabundance"
)

# Quantify dissimilarities in the ordination space
dp <- as.matrix(dist(reducedDim(tse, "PCoA")))

# Calculate stress i.e. relative difference
# in the original and projected dissimilarities
stress <- sum((dp - d0)^2) / sum(d0^2)
```

A Shepard plot visualizes the original versus the ordinated dissimilarity
between the observations (@fig-community-shepard).

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-shepard
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"
#| fig-cap: "Shepard plot comparing the original Bray-Curtis dissimilarities (x-axis) with the distances in the PCoA space (y-axis) for the GlobalPatterns samples. The relative stress is shown in the subtitle."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot with the original Bray-Curtis dissimilarity on the x-axis and the distance in the PCoA space on the y-axis, one point per sample pair. The subtitle gives the stress value."

ord <- order(as.vector(d0))
df <- data.frame(
    d0 = as.vector(d0)[ord],
    dmds = as.vector(dp)[ord]
)

ggplot(df, aes(x = d0, y = dmds)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
    labs(
        x = "Original distance",
        y = "MDS distance",
        subtitle = paste("Stress:", round(stress, 2))
    )
```

## Constrained ordination

dbRDA is a supervised counterpart of PCoA. It maximizes the variance with
respect to the covariates provided by the user. This can be used to quantify
associations between each covariate and community composition (beta diversity).
The table below summarizes the relations between the supervised and
unsupervised ordination methods.

|                          | supervised ordination  | unsupervised ordination  |
|:------------------------:|:----------------------:|:------------------------:|
| Euclidean distance       | RDA                    | PCA                      |
| non-Euclidean distance   | dbRDA                  | PCoA/MDS, NMDS           |

In summary, the "dbRDA" is the more general method that allows a wider
variety of dissimilarity, or beta diversity, indices. This method is available
via `mia::getRDA()`, which calls `vegan::dbrda()`. By default, this uses
Euclidean distances, which is equivalent to the ordinary RDA. However, the
dbRDA method (`mia::getRDA()`) allows the use of other dissimilarity indices as
well.

Let us next demonstrate dbRDA with the enterotype dataset [@Arumugam2011]
([@sec-data-enterotype]). Here samples
correspond to patients. The `colData` lists the clinical status of each patient
and a few covariates such as gender and age.

```{r}
#| label: import_rda_dataset

# Load data
data("enterotype", package = "mia")
tse2 <- enterotype
rownames(tse2)[rownames(tse2) == "-1"] <- "Unassigned"

# Apply relative transform
tse2 <- transformAssay(tse2, method = "relabundance")
```

### Redundancy analysis

dbRDA can be performed with the `addRDA()` function. In addition to the
arguments previously defined for
[unsupervised ordination](#sec-unsupervised-ordination),
this function takes a formula to control for variables and an action to treat
missing values. Along with clinical status, which is the main outcome, we
control for gender and age, and exclude observations where one of these
variables is missing.

```{r}
#| label: run_rda

# Perform RDA
set.seed(123)
tse2 <- addRDA(
    tse2,
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    formula = assay ~ ClinicalStatus + Gender + Age,
    distance = "bray",
    na.action = na.exclude
)

# Store results of PERMANOVA test
rda_info <- attr(reducedDim(tse2, "RDA"), "significance")
```

The importance of each variable on the similarity between samples (i.e.,
loadings) can be assessed from the results of PERMANOVA, automatically provided
by the `addRDA()` function. It first performs dbRDA and then applies
permutational tests to its results.

As previously described, [PERMANOVA](#sec-permanova) is a widely used
non-parametric multivariate method that aims to estimate the actual statistical
significance of differences in the observed community composition between
groups of samples (here, the five clinical status groups). PERMANOVA tests the
hypothesis that the centroids of the community are equivalent between the
compared groups. A p-value smaller than the significance threshold indicates
that the groups have a different community composition, provided that the
group dispersions are homogeneous (see below).

This method is implemented with the
[`adonis2`](https://vegandevs.github.io/vegan/reference/adonis.html)
function from the `r BiocStyle::CRANpkg("vegan")` package.

From the results table below, we see that both clinical status and age explain
more than 10% of the variance, however, only age has statistical significance.

```{r}
#| label: rda_permanova_results

rda_info$permanova |>
    knitr::kable()
```

Next, we proceed to visualize the weight and significance of each variable on
the similarity between samples with an RDA plot, which can be generated with
the `plotRDA()` function from the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("miaViz")` package
(@fig-community-rda).

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-rda
#| fig-cap: "dbRDA plot of the enterotype dataset with samples colored by clinical status. Arrows show the contributions of the covariates clinical status, gender and age."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of the samples on the first two dbRDA axes, with points colored by clinical status. Arrows from the origin show the directions of the covariates clinical status, gender and age."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

# Load packages for plotting function
library(miaViz)

# Generate RDA plot colored by clinical status
plotRDA(tse2, "RDA", colour.by = "ClinicalStatus") +
    labs(colour = "Clinical status")
```

From above, we can see that only age significantly describes differences
between the microbial profiles of different samples. Such visual approach
complements the previous results obtained with PERMANOVA.

::: {.callout-tip }
## Speed up calculations

Calculating dissimilarities between samples is a computationally demanding
task, which can make methods like dbRDA or PCoA time-consuming with large
datasets. To speed up calculations, consider using functions that support
parallel processing instead of the default `r BiocStyle::CRANpkg("vegan")`
package options. Packages like `r BiocStyle::CRANpkg("parallelDist")`
can significantly improve performance on systems with multiple available cores.

In `*Dissimilarity()` functions, you can specify the utilized dissimilarity
function with `dis.fun` argument.

```
tse <- addDissimilarity(
    tse,
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    method = "bray",
    dis.fun = parallelDist::parallelDist
)
```

This same approach can also be used in PCoA.

```
tse <- addMDS(
    tse,
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    method = "bray",
    dis.fun = parallelDist::parallelDist
)
```

With dbRDA, you can use precomputed dissimilarity matrices, allowing the method
to bypass the dissimilarity estimation step. This enhances efficiency and
speeds up the analysis.

```
tse <- addRDA(
    tse,
    dis.name = "bray",
    formula = assay ~ ClinicalStatus + Gender + Age,
    na.action = na.exclude
)
```

:::

### dbRDA loadings {#sec-dbrda-workflow}

Let us visualize the model coefficients or loadings for species that exhibit
the largest differences between the groups. This gives some insights into how
the groups tend to differ from each other in terms of community composition
(@fig-community-rda-loadings).

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-rda-loadings
#| fig-cap: "Loadings of the 20 taxa with the largest contributions to the first two dbRDA components in the enterotype dataset."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels of horizontal bar charts, one for each of the first two dbRDA components, with the 20 taxa on the y-axis and their loadings on the x-axis."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

plotLoadings(tse2, "RDA", ncomponents = 2, n = 20)
```

```{r}
#| label: get_top_taxa
#| echo: false

loadings <- attr(reducedDim(tse2, "RDA"), "species")
top_coef <- sort(abs(loadings[, 1]), decreasing = TRUE)
```

In the example above, the largest contributions to the first dbRDA component
can be attributed to _`r names(top_coef)[[1]]`_ and _`r names(top_coef)[[2]]`_.

### Homogeneity check

It is important to note that the application of PERMANOVA assumes homogeneous
group dispersions (variances). This can be tested with the PERMDISP2 method
[@Anderson2006] by using the same assay and distance method as in PERMANOVA.

To ensure that the homogeneity assumption holds, we retrieve the corresponding
information from the results of RDA. Group dispersions are only defined for
categorical variables, so we show the results for clinical status and gender.
`addRDA()` also tests age, but because age is continuous, each distinct value
is treated as its own group, and that result is not meaningful. None of the
p-values of the categorical variables is lower than the significance
threshold, and thus homogeneity is observed.

::: {.callout-note}
## Note

PERMANOVA assumes that the group dispersions are homogeneous. This means that
the variation within groups, i.e., the spread of samples around their group
centroid, is similar in all groups. If this assumption is not met, the results
can be misleading.

`addRDA()` performs homogeneity test automatically.
:::

```{r}
#| label: rda_homogeneity_results

# Homogeneity of dispersion is defined only for categorical variables
rda_info$homogeneity[c("ClinicalStatus", "Gender"), ] |>
    knitr::kable()
```

As the group dispersions are homogeneous, PERMANOVA can be seen as an
appropriate choice for comparing community compositions.

## Case studies

### Visualizing the most dominant genus on PCoA {#sec-pcoa-genus}

In this section, we visualize the most dominant genus with PCoA. A similar
visualization was proposed by @Salosensaari2021. First, let us agglomerate the
data at the Genus level and identify the dominant taxonomic features for each
sample.

```{r}
#| label: case_study1

# Agglomerate to genus level
tse_genus <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "Genus")

# Convert to relative abundances
tse_genus <- transformAssay(
    tse_genus,
    method = "relabundance", assay.type = "counts"
)

# Add info on dominant genus per sample
tse_genus <- addDominant(
    tse_genus,
    assay.type = "relabundance", name = "dominant_taxa"
)

# Overview
summarizeDominance(
    tse_genus,
    digits = 3, name = "dominant_taxa"
)
```

Next, we perform PCoA with Bray-Curtis dissimilarity.

```{r}
#| label: case_study2

tse_genus <- addMDS(
    tse_genus,
    name = "PCoA_BC",
    method = "bray",
    assay.type = "relabundance"
)
```

Finally, we visualize the dominant genera on the PCoA
(@fig-community-pcoa-dominant).

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-pcoa-dominant
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"
#| fig-cap: "Bray-Curtis PCoA of the GlobalPatterns samples colored by their dominant genus. The six genera that are most often dominant are shown separately and the remaining genera are grouped as Other."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of the samples on the first two PCoA axes, with the percentage of variance explained in the axis labels. Points are colored by dominant genus, with seven colors for the six most often dominant genera and Other."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

# Dominant genus of each sample. Genera other than the six most often
# dominant ones are named "Other".
tse_genus <- addDominant(
    tse_genus,
    assay.type = "relabundance", n = 6, name = "most_abundant"
)

# Visualization
plotOrdination(
    tse_genus, "PCoA_BC",
    colour.by = "most_abundant",
    add.expl.var = TRUE
) +
    labs(colour = "Most abundant genus")
```

Similarly, we visualize and compare the sub-population
(@fig-community-pcoa-dominant-groups).

```{r}
#| label: fig-community-pcoa-dominant-groups
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"
#| fig-cap: "Bray-Curtis PCoA of the GlobalPatterns samples colored by their dominant genus, shown separately for fecal and non-fecal samples."
#| fig-alt: "Two scatter plots side by side, one for fecal and one for non-fecal samples, showing the samples on the first two PCoA axes. Points are colored by dominant genus, using the six most often dominant genera and Other."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

# Visualization split by group
plotOrdination(
    tse_genus, "PCoA_BC",
    colour.by = "most_abundant",
    facet.by = "Group",
    add.expl.var = TRUE
) +
    labs(colour = "Most abundant genus")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Functions for dissimilarity and ordination

As a final note, we provide a comprehensive list of functions for the
evaluation of dissimilarity indices available in the
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("mia")` and `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("scater")`
packages. The `get` (and `calculate`) methods return the result, such as a
matrix of reduced dimensions, as an output, whereas the `add` (and `run`)
methods store the result into the specified `TreeSE`.

* Canonical Correspondence Analysis (CCA) [@terBraak1986]: `getCCA()` and
`addCCA()`
* dbRDA: `getRDA()` and `addRDA()`; our recommended default method to assess
differences in community composition (beta diversity)
* Double Principal Coordinate Analysis (DPCoA) [@Pavoine2004]: `getDPCoA()`
and `addDPCoA()`
* Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) [@Lin1991]: `getDissimilarity()` and
`addDissimilarity()` with `method = "jsd"`
* MDS: `getMDS()` and `addMDS()`
* NMDS: `getNMDS()` and `addNMDS()`
* Overlap: `getDissimilarity()` and `addDissimilarity()` with
`method = "overlap"`
* PERMANOVA: `getPERMANOVA()` and `addPERMANOVA()` (based on
`vegan::adonis2()`) can be used to assess significance
when comparing community composition between groups. However, retrieving the
loadings and components is more tricky.
* t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) [@vanderMaaten2008]:
`calculateTSNE()` and `runTSNE()` (not commonly used for microbiome data)
* UMAP [@McInnes2018]: `calculateUMAP()` and `runUMAP()` (not commonly used for
microbiome data)

For more information on sample clustering, you can refer to:

* [How to extract information from clusters](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSCA.basic/clustering.html)
* [@sec-clustering] on community typing
:::

## Exercises {#sec-community-similarity-exercises}

We use the [`Tengeler2020`](data_sets.qmd#sec-data-tengeler2020) dataset.

Solve the exercises in order, as each exercise continues from the previous
one. Try to solve each exercise yourself before opening the solution.

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 1: Dissimilarity metrics

**Goal:** Explain how the choice of dissimilarity metric affects what is
compared between samples.

Imagine two samples that both contain the same three taxa and 100 reads in
total:

| Taxon   | Sample A | Sample B |
|---------|---------:|---------:|
| Taxon 1 | 50       | 5        |
| Taxon 2 | 30       | 5        |
| Taxon 3 | 20       | 90       |

Answer the following questions without writing any code. The beginning of
this chapter and the callouts "Dissimilarity or distance?" and "Common mistake
in Jaccard index" will help you.

1. What is the (presence/absence) Jaccard dissimilarity between the samples?

2. Would the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between the samples be the same as the
Jaccard dissimilarity? Why?

3. Which metric would you choose if you wanted to take into account how
closely related the taxa are in the phylogenetic tree?

4. The Aitchison distance can be calculated as a Euclidean distance. Which
transformation must be applied to the counts first?

5. Is Bray-Curtis a distance or a dissimilarity?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

1. The Jaccard dissimilarity is 0. The presence/absence Jaccard index only
compares which taxa are present, and both samples contain the same three taxa.

2. No. Bray-Curtis takes the abundances of the taxa into account. The samples
contain the same taxa, but in very different proportions, so the Bray-Curtis
dissimilarity is larger than zero, whereas the Jaccard dissimilarity is zero.

3. UniFrac, which uses the phylogenetic tree of the taxa.

4. The centered log-ratio (clr) transformation. The Aitchison distance is the
Euclidean distance between clr-transformed abundances.

5. Bray-Curtis is a dissimilarity. It does not fulfill all the requirements
of a distance metric.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 2: Dissimilarity and divergence

**Goal:** Calculate and visualize the dissimilarities between samples, and the
divergence of each sample from a reference.

1. Load the `Tengeler2020` dataset from the `mia` package and store it in a
variable called `tse`.

2. Transform the `counts` assay to relative abundances. The new assay is
called `relabundance`.

3. Calculate the Bray-Curtis dissimilarities between the samples from the
`relabundance` assay with `addDissimilarity()`. Check the names of
`metadata(tse)`. Where was the result stored?

4. Visualize the dissimilarity matrix as a heatmap, and annotate the samples
by `patient_status`.

5. Calculate the divergence of each sample from the median sample with
`addDivergence()`. Use the `relabundance` assay, `reference = "median"` and
`method = "bray"`. The result is stored in the `divergence` column of
`colData`.

6. Visualize the divergence as boxplots, with one box for each group in
`patient_status`.

7. What does a single value in the dissimilarity matrix tell? What does a
high divergence tell about a sample?

**Useful functions:** `data()`, `mia::transformAssay()`,
`mia::addDissimilarity()`, `metadata()`, `miaViz::plotDissimilarity()`,
`mia::addDivergence()`, `miaViz::plotBoxplot()`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise_community_dissimilarity
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

library(mia)
library(miaViz)

# 1. Load the data
data("Tengeler2020", package = "mia")
tse <- Tengeler2020

# 2. Relative abundances
tse <- transformAssay(tse, assay.type = "counts", method = "relabundance")

# 3. Bray-Curtis dissimilarities, stored in metadata
tse <- addDissimilarity(tse, assay.type = "relabundance", method = "bray")
names(metadata(tse))

# 4. Heatmap of the dissimilarities
plotDissimilarity(tse, name = "bray", col.var = "patient_status")

# 5. Divergence from the median sample
tse <- addDivergence(
    tse,
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    reference = "median",
    method = "bray"
)

# 6. Boxplot of divergence by group
plotBoxplot(tse, col.var = "divergence", x = "patient_status") +
    labs(x = "Patient status", y = "Divergence from the median")
```

3. The dissimilarity matrix was stored in `metadata(tse)` under the name
`bray`.

<!-- -->

7. Each value in the dissimilarity matrix compares one pair of samples. A
value close to 0 means that the two communities are very similar, and a value
close to 1 means that they share hardly any abundance. The divergence
compares a sample to a reference, here the median sample. A high divergence
means that the community of the sample differs much from the typical
community in the data.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 3: Principal Coordinate Analysis (PCoA)

**Goal:** Run PCoA and compare how the choice of dissimilarity metric and assay
affects the ordination.

1. Run PCoA with `addMDS()` on the `relabundance` assay using Bray-Curtis
dissimilarity. Store the result under the name `"MDS_bray"`.

2. List the names of the reduced dimensions stored in `tse`. Is `"MDS_bray"`
among them?

3. Plot the first two coordinates of `"MDS_bray"` and color the samples by
`patient_status`.

4. Apply the clr transformation to the `counts` assay with a pseudocount of
0.5. Then run PCoA on the `clr` assay with Euclidean
distance, that is, with the Aitchison distance. Store the result under the
name `"MDS_aitchison"`.

5. Plot the first two coordinates of `"MDS_aitchison"` and color the samples
by `patient_status`. Compare the plot with the plot from step 3.

6. How do you read a PCoA plot? Why can the two plots look different, even
though they are based on the same samples?

**Useful functions:** `mia::addMDS()`, `mia::getDissimilarity()`,
`SingleCellExperiment::reducedDimNames()`, `miaViz::plotOrdination()`,
`mia::transformAssay()`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise_community_pcoa
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

library(miaViz)

# 1. PCoA with Bray-Curtis dissimilarity
tse <- addMDS(
    tse,
    method = "bray",
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    name = "MDS_bray"
)

# 2. Names of the reduced dimensions
reducedDimNames(tse)

# 3. Plot the Bray-Curtis PCoA
plotOrdination(tse, "MDS_bray", colour.by = "patient_status") +
    labs(colour = "Patient status")

# 4. clr transformation and PCoA with Aitchison distance
tse <- transformAssay(
    tse,
    assay.type = "counts", method = "clr", pseudocount = 0.5
)
tse <- addMDS(
    tse,
    method = "euclidean",
    assay.type = "clr",
    name = "MDS_aitchison"
)

# 5. Plot the Aitchison PCoA
plotOrdination(tse, "MDS_aitchison", colour.by = "patient_status") +
    labs(colour = "Patient status")
```

6. Each point is a sample. Samples that are close to each other have similar
community compositions, and samples that are far apart have different
compositions. If the samples of a group cluster together and apart from the
other group, the groups differ in community composition. If the groups
overlap, the ordination does not show a clear difference. The two plots are
based on different metrics. Bray-Curtis on relative abundances is dominated
by the most abundant taxa. The Aitchison distance compares log-ratios, so a
relative (fold) change counts equally regardless of the abundance of the
taxon, and rare taxa have more influence than in Bray-Curtis. Therefore,
the metric and assay should be chosen to fit the research question.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 4: Rarefaction in PCoA

**Goal:** Account for uneven sequencing depth with rarefaction in ordination.

1. Calculate the library size of each sample, that is, the total number of
reads in each sample, and summarize the library sizes.

2. Run PCoA with Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and rarefaction. Use the `counts`
assay, set the rarefaction depth `sample` to the smallest library size, use
`niter = 10` iterations, and store the result under the name
`"MDS_bray_rarefied"`. Set a seed before running the PCoA, as rarefaction is
random.

3. Plot the first two coordinates of `"MDS_bray_rarefied"` and color the
samples by `patient_status`. Compare the plot with the `"MDS_bray"` plot from
Exercise 3.

4. Why do we rarefy, and why do we use the smallest library size as the
rarefaction depth?

**Useful functions:** `assay()`, `colSums()`, `summary()`, `min()`,
`set.seed()`, `mia::addMDS()`, `mia::getDissimilarity()`,
`miaViz::plotOrdination()`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise_community_rarefaction
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

# 1. Library sizes
lib_size <- colSums(assay(tse, "counts"))
summary(lib_size)

# 2. PCoA with rarefaction
set.seed(123)
tse <- addMDS(
    tse,
    method = "bray",
    assay.type = "counts",
    sample = min(lib_size),
    niter = 10,
    name = "MDS_bray_rarefied"
)

# 3. Plot the rarefied PCoA
plotOrdination(tse, "MDS_bray_rarefied", colour.by = "patient_status") +
    labs(colour = "Patient status")
```

4. Samples with more reads tend to have more taxa detected, so part of the
differences between samples can be due to sequencing depth. Rarefaction
subsamples every sample to the same number of reads, and the dissimilarities
are averaged over the iterations. A sample cannot be subsampled to more reads
than it contains, so samples with fewer reads than the chosen depth would
have to be removed. Using the smallest library size keeps all the samples.
If the rarefied and non-rarefied plots look similar, the differences in
sequencing depth have little effect on the ordination. If they look
different, sequencing depth affects the result. Note that PCoA axes can be
flipped between runs, so compare the relative positions of the samples
rather than the signs of the coordinates.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 5: PERMANOVA

**Goal:** Test whether a variable explains differences in community composition,
and check the homogeneity of group dispersions.

1. Set a seed, as PERMANOVA is based on random permutations. Then run
PERMANOVA with `getPERMANOVA()` on the `relabundance` assay with Bray-Curtis
dissimilarity and the formula `x ~ patient_status`. Store the result in
`res`.

2. Look at the `permanova` table of the result. Find the proportion of
variance explained (`R2`) by `patient_status` and the p-value (`Pr(>F)`).

3. Look at the `homogeneity` table of the result. What does this test
measure?

4. Why should the homogeneity of group dispersions be checked when
interpreting PERMANOVA?

**Useful functions:** `set.seed()`, `mia::getPERMANOVA()`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise_community_permanova

# 1. PERMANOVA
set.seed(123)
res <- getPERMANOVA(
    tse,
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    method = "bray",
    formula = x ~ patient_status
)

# 2. PERMANOVA results
res$permanova

# 3. Homogeneity of group dispersions
res$homogeneity
```

2. `R2` tells the proportion of the variation in community composition that
`patient_status` explains, and `Pr(>F)` is the permutation p-value. A p-value
below the significance threshold (e.g. 0.05) means that the group centroids
differ more than would be expected by chance.

3. The homogeneity test compares the group dispersions, that is, the average
distances between the samples and their group centroid.

4. PERMANOVA compares the group centroids and assumes that the dispersions
of the groups are similar. A significant PERMANOVA result together with a
non-significant homogeneity test supports a difference in composition between
the groups. If the homogeneity test is also significant, the PERMANOVA result
may be caused by differences in the within-group variability instead, and it
should be interpreted with caution.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 6: Distance-based redundancy analysis (dbRDA)

**Goal:** Run dbRDA with several covariates and visualize the result.

1. Set a seed. Then run dbRDA with `addRDA()` on the `relabundance` assay
with Bray-Curtis dissimilarity (`distance = "bray"`) and the formula
`assay ~ patient_status + cohort`.

2. Retrieve the `"significance"` attribute of the `"RDA"` reduced dimension
and store it in `rda_info`. Look at its `permanova` and `homogeneity`
tables.

3. Visualize the dbRDA result and color the samples by `patient_status`.

4. Visualize the loadings of the 10 taxa with the largest contributions to
the first two dbRDA components.

5. Why do we include `cohort` in the formula? How do you read the arrows in
the dbRDA plot?

**Useful functions:** `set.seed()`, `mia::addRDA()`, `attr()`,
`SingleCellExperiment::reducedDim()`, `miaViz::plotRDA()`,
`miaViz::plotLoadings()`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise_community_dbrda
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

# 1. dbRDA with two covariates
set.seed(123)
tse <- addRDA(
    tse,
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    formula = assay ~ patient_status + cohort,
    distance = "bray"
)

# 2. PERMANOVA and homogeneity results
rda_info <- attr(reducedDim(tse, "RDA"), "significance")
rda_info$permanova
rda_info$homogeneity

# 3. dbRDA plot
plotRDA(tse, "RDA", colour.by = "patient_status") +
    labs(colour = "Patient status")

# 4. Loadings of the top 10 taxa
plotLoadings(tse, "RDA", ncomponents = 2, n = 10)
```

5. The mice come from different cohorts, and the cohort may also affect
community composition. When `cohort` is included in the formula, the effect
of `patient_status` is estimated while controlling for cohort, and the
`permanova` table shows the variance explained by each variable separately.
In the dbRDA plot, each arrow shows a covariate. For a categorical variable,
there is one arrow for each level, compared to the reference level. The
direction of an arrow shows in which direction the samples differ along that
covariate, and a longer arrow means a stronger association with community
composition. The labels show the explained variance and the p-value of each
variable.
:::
::::
